name: Liam Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Morning starts with a prayer, then the school run for Yusuf and Maryam, then I'm at Fenwick Catering Supplies by eight. We sell ovens, fridges, dishwashers, pans and tableware to restaurants, hotels and hospital kitchens, and I buy the whole range from about eighty makers. I use an AI assistant every day to compare quotes and draft emails, and then I spend the real time on the deals: how many fryers to commit to before the autumn rush. I love closing a good deal. What wears me out is that restaurants fail a lot, and when they do, we're left holding the debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, so we keep the tools we've got and work harder. At work I'd tell the team the tools help, the hype was too much, and the money is in the deals. At the mosque I'd say work hard and trust in God. Online, nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd say my edge stays, since I'm already faster with the tools than most. But I'd be a bit bored, and I'd feel there's less to build. The pressure I already carry is the bad-debt risk. A good restaurant customer that fails costs us thousands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the assistant for quotes and credit checks, and I'd tighten how we judge customers. I'd put another 600 a month into a property fund with my brother-in-law, because I like owning things. And I'd keep studying the trade: new oven makers, energy-saving kitchens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. A little restless. I like change, and a plateau is a bit flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said restaurant failures leave you with debts. Does a plateau change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say do it, but start small. In a quiet world, the winners are the ones who watch costs and treat customers well. I'd tell them what I learned: never give credit to anyone you wouldn't lend your car to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who wants to start a business in a quiet world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A plateau doesn't touch that. Restaurant failures are about rent, energy and wages, not AI. I use the tool to check credit risk, which helps, but it's not perfect. We lost about 40,000 last year to two customers, and I took that personally.

say: Keep the **tools** we've got, work harder, and the money is in the deals.
think: My **edge** stays, though I'd feel a bit bored and restless.
The pressure I already carry is **bad debt**, because a failed restaurant costs us thousands.
do: Use the assistant for quotes and **credit checks**, and tighten how we judge customers.
Put another **600 a month** into a property fund with my brother-in-law.
feel: **Good**, a little restless, since a plateau is a bit flat.
S0.quote: Never give credit to anyone you wouldn't lend your car to.
fieldNote: Liam's **adaptive** style means a plateau just means more of the same, with some boredom.
Bad debt is his **real** pressure, and the 40,000 loss last year still bothers him.

steps.text: Use the assistant for credit checks on new customers
Put another 600 a month into a property fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say good, let's lead on this and not be dragged. To friends I'd say learn the tools now, because those who do will have the jobs. At the mosque I'd say help the young and the old who don't pick it up easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm excited. The routine of buying, the quote comparison and the forecasting go to software, and I'll be among the first to use it well. But I'm honest with myself: some of my team will go, and I may be the one who has to choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put myself in charge of the rollout at Fenwick. I'd automate quote comparison and the first draft of orders, and keep myself on the big deals and the customer relationships. I'd start a small side project too, selling used kitchen equipment online, because those tools make it easy. And I'd keep investing every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, with a weight on my chest about the team. I'd say about seventy-thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you build with these tools that you can't now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build an assistant that watches every customer's payments and warns us before they fail. It would save us tens of thousands a year. I'd also build one that tells restaurant owners what equipment they'd need if they open a second site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our admin and junior buyers: Salma, Peter and Ravi. They do the routine and I'd want to help them move into customer roles or training. I'd say to the owners, give them a year of paid retraining. Paid retraining for my team is cheaper than redundancy, and it's right.

say: Let's **lead** on this and not be dragged.
Help the young and the old who don't pick it up **easily**.
think: I'm **excited**, but some of my team will go and I may have to choose.
I'll be among the first to use it **well**.
do: Take charge of the **rollout** and automate quote comparison and first-draft orders.
Start a **side project** selling used kitchen equipment online.
feel: Mostly **excited**, with a weight on my chest about the team.
S1.quote: Paid retraining for my team is cheaper than redundancy, and it's right.
fieldNote: Liam's **adaptive** edge shows in leading the rollout and starting a side business.
He cares about **Salma, Peter and Ravi**, and pushes paid retraining, a traditional sense of duty.

steps.text: Lead the tool rollout at Fenwick
Sell used kitchen equipment online on the side
Argue for a year of paid retraining for the junior buyers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to act now: costs down, plan up, and keep our people. To friends I'd say the world is changing and we should hold together. At the mosque I'd say trust in God and look after your neighbour. Online I'd say this should be a matter for families and communities, and for government to keep out of the way of small business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the real thing. When AI does all thinking work, a buyer isn't needed, even one who is good with the tools. I'd say my edge goes in two years. I'm not panicking, though, because I think there will still be a chance to own things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Day one, I'd count our cash and cut all the extras. Then I'd try to buy a small stake in something with hands-on elements: a kitchen equipment installer or a catering hire firm. I'd talk to Amina about the nursery. And I'd get my savings out of anything that depends on office work. I'd also push Fenwick to let me move into customer-facing sales, where people still want a handshake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan, so more like focused. There's a fear underneath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on day one with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Amina runs a children's nursery, so her work is hands-on and lasts at least three more years after mine. That's a big comfort. It's also very modest pay, so we couldn't live on it, and I'd feel the weight of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Amina's work as a nursery manager change things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd count the cash: about eleven months of expenses. Then I'd call my brother-in-law about the installer business. A hands-on business is where I'd want to be when thinking work goes.

say: We need to act now: **costs down**, plan up, and keep our people.
Government should keep out of the way of **small business**.
think: When AI does all thinking work a buyer isn't needed, so my **edge** goes in two years.
I'm not panicking, because there will still be a chance to **own** things.
do: Count our **cash**, cut the extras, and try to buy a stake in a kitchen installer or hire firm.
Push Fenwick to move me into customer-facing **sales**.
feel: **Anxious**, but more focused than frightened, with a fear underneath.
S2.quote: A hands-on business is where I'd want to be when thinking work goes.
fieldNote: Liam's answer to AGI is **ownership** of something hands-on, a practical and entrepreneurial reflex.
Amina's **nursery** lasts longer but pays modestly, so it doesn't solve the money question.

steps.text: Cut all the extras and count eleven months of cash
Buy a small stake in a kitchen installer
Ask Fenwick to move me into customer-facing sales
Move savings out of anything tied to office work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is a good run, so let's prepare. To friends I'd say get a skill that lasts, or own something. At the mosque I'd say be generous, and look after each other. Online I'd say back small business and apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is a window, and I'd use it. I'd be 48, with a strong cushion. I think I can build something of my own: a small distribution or installation business, using the tools to run it with a handful of people. I'm uneasy, but also sort of keen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools hard for two years to build up Fenwick's systems and my own reputation. Then I'd buy into a hands-on business, maybe with my brother-in-law, and move over by year three. I'd put money into property, and I'd teach Yusuf the basics of business, and a trade, as I'd want him to have both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit excited. I'd call it ambition with a seatbelt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in those five years that you'd rush in two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be forced to make a quick bet. With five, I can choose a good one. I'd test it first, a side business at weekends, and see if it works before I leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in wholesale?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not as a buyer, but maybe in wholesale as an owner. That's different. A small owner with a good system and good relationships has a place, but an employee buyer doesn't.

say: Five years is a good run, so let's **prepare**.
Back **small business** and apprenticeships, because those build real skills and real jobs.
think: Five years is a **window**, and I think I can build something of my own.
do: Use the tools hard for two years, then buy into a **hands-on** business by year three.
Teach Yusuf the basics of **business** and a trade.
feel: **Uneasy** and a bit excited, ambition with a seatbelt.
S3.quote: A small owner with a good system and good relationships has a place, but an employee buyer doesn't.
fieldNote: Liam has a **sequence**: build systems, then buy into a hands-on firm by year three.
He would **test** the idea first at weekends, which fits his careful risk-taking.

steps.text: Build Fenwick's buying systems and my reputation for two years
Test a weekend side business before leaving
Buy into a hands-on business by year three
Teach Yusuf the basics of business and a trade

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say a decade is a lot of time, so let's build well. To friends I'd say start now, don't wait for year nine. At the mosque I'd say teach children good habits. Online I'd say keep taxes low, and make it easy to start things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm calm. I'll be 53, with strong savings and the habit of learning. I'd like to own a business by then, because a decade is plenty to grow one. I'd say it's a gift of time, if you use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and keep learning. I'd build my own business in the second year, maybe a small installer or distribution firm, and grow it steadily. I'd keep investing and pay down the mortgage. I'd also volunteer in our community, helping young people get apprenticeships, because that's how I'd like to give back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and ambitious. A decade is a big canvas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd build rather than rescue. I'd get it right, with good partners, good systems and a name that people trust. I wouldn't need to rush into anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you talk to your children about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Yusuf and Maryam that work is honour, that skills matter, and that the world will change. Be curious, be kind, and have something you can do with your hands. I'd say tools are good servants and bad masters.

say: A decade is a lot of time, so let's **build well**.
Start now, don't wait for **year nine**.
think: I'm **calm**, at 53 with strong savings and the habit of learning.
A decade is plenty to **grow** a business, a gift of time if you use it.
do: Start my own small **installer or distribution** firm in the second year and grow it steadily.
Volunteer helping young people into **apprenticeships**, and pay down the mortgage.
feel: **Calm** and ambitious, with a decade as a big canvas.
S4.quote: Tools are good servants and bad masters.
fieldNote: Liam sees ten years as time to **build** rather than rescue, a very entrepreneurial reading.
His **duty** to community, through apprenticeships, links to his traditional values.

steps.text: Start a small installer or distribution business in year two
Volunteer with a local apprenticeship scheme
Teach Yusuf and Maryam a hands-on skill

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it leaves almost no time to move from buying into something I own, and my edge from knowing the tools goes away. What would help is a fair tax and rules climate for small businesses, apprenticeships and training that lead to real work, and employers who give notice. I'd rather build than be given.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that adaptable people aren't automatically fine. I use the tools every day and I still feel the pull of the clock.

headlineQuote: I use the tools every day and I still feel the pull of the clock.
portrait: Liam is a 43-year-old senior **catering equipment buyer** at Fenwick, with a nursery-manager partner, two children and a mortgage.
He is traditional and **adaptive**: he uses AI daily, believes in free markets, faith and apprenticeships.
His mood is calm in mild worlds, **anxious** at two years, and he reaches for ownership of something hands-on.
He plans a **side business**, buys into a hands-on firm, and mentors young people into trades.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario, because there is almost no time to move from buying into ownership.
whatWouldHelp: A fair climate for **small business**, apprenticeships that lead to real work, and notice from employers.
